<reason>Side B won the decisive clash. B's pressure on enforcement and retention forced A into two honest concessions (the sanction is financial; there is no mechanism keeping the relocated applicant in place), then B converted those concessions into a weighing story: a fully-enforced quota yields money for frontline capacity, i.e. B's own model purchased at the extra price of litigation, defiance, and nationalist backlash. B also landed a factual correction A never repaired—relocation occurs after landing and registration, so "he never lands on Lesbos" was wrong and Greece still does the hardest work. A's counter-framing (default obligation vs. negotiated charity, frontline states' own preference, "relief that arrives without sharing is a receipt") was genuinely strong and gave A a live route, and A's A1/A2 answers were direct and candid rather than evasive. But A never neutralized the retention problem beyond "who absorbs the leak," and B's closing crystallization ("the same relief, purchased twice: once in cash, once in cohesion") was the cleaner reason to vote. B's clipped opening and rebuttal were minor execution costs, and A's "most member states did relocate" claim sat on shaky ground.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 (B4.1–B4.5): after A conceded the sanction was a fine that funds reception capacity, B answered A's two pressure questions and then turned the concessions—"my mechanism, endorsed"—and corrected A's false comfort that relocation prevents Lesbos landings, collapsing A's case into flexible solidarity plus a court summons.</best_rebuttal>
